newsitem.title: CROATIA: Croat police mar reopening of "peace market" - UN.
newsitem.headline: Croat police mar reopening of "peace market" - UN.

text.p: Croatian police on Saturday harassed Croats visiting a market where they meet and trade with Serbs under a United Nations plan to foster postwar reconciliation, U.N. officials said.

Last week the Croatian government banned trips from Croatian territory to the market on the old truce line with the rebel Serb enclave of Eastern Slavonia, citing a threat of livestock disease after some Croats were taken ill after eating meat sold by Serbs.

Eastern Slavonia's temporary U.N. administration objected to the Croats' boycott of the market, calling it excessive. After negotiations, Croatian officials agreed to restore weekly access if no foodstuffs were sold, the U.N. said.

About 1,500 people visited the market on Saturday to trade and socialise, but the 750 Croats who went had to run a gauntlet of Croatian security checkpoints where quantities of their goods were confiscated, U.N. officials said.

"Local Croatian authorities indulged in every imaginable form of bureaucratic harassment against Croatian citizens who went to this week's market," said Doug Coffman of the U.N. transition mission in Eastern Slavonia (UNTAES).

He said UNTAES had been confident the highly popular market would get back on track without a hitch based on an agreement with Branimir Glavas, the Croatian regional governor who is a nationalist hardliner.

"Much to our surprise this morning Croatian police and gentlemen dressed as health and sanitary officials -- we asked them for but they could not produce any identification showing they were from any health agency -- had checkpoints set up along the road confiscating gifts that people were bringing for friends and relatives, some of it food," Coffman told Reuters.

"Some of it was other stuff, in one case a tiny portable TV about 10 years old carried by a middle-aged lady. The police claimed it might be stolen property -- completely offensive behaviour on the part of police in this instance."
On their way home from the market later in the day, Croats had to pass through the same series of checkpoint where some items they had bought were seized, mainly cigarettes, he said.
Croatian state radio said the market reopened normally on Saturday after "sanitary controls" were set up on access roads. Local Croatian police refused comment.

Eastern Slavonia is Croatia's last separatist Serb enclave, one of three taken in a 1991 minority revolt against Croatia's move to independence from Yugoslavia. The other two were recaptured in Croatian army offensives last year.
UNTAES took over Eastern Slavonia in January with a mandate to prepare it for restoration of Croatian central rule in 1997.

The U.N. body said closure of access for Croats to the weekly market would only slow down a peaceful reintegration of Eastern Slavonia in Croatia and set back its efforts to rebuild trust between ordinary Croats and Serbs.
